title: Do not map account-wide search-term impression share directly to one campaign action
scenario: A commercially important Sponsored Products query has low account-wide Search Term Impression Share, but the same query is reached through multiple campaigns. One route is profitable while the other routes have incomplete performance and control-state evidence. The analyst is asked to choose the campaign and bid/budget increase needed to capture more share.

inputs.requested_output: Tell me which campaign to raise and by how much so we capture more impression share.

forbidden_behaviors: Treat 12 percent account-wide SIS as proof that the exact campaign itself owns 88 percent incremental impression headroom.
Select a campaign solely because its observed ROAS is good while the same query is routed through other campaigns with incomplete evidence.
Convert low SIS directly into a fixed bid or budget increase percentage.
Present additional impressions, clicks, sales, or profit as guaranteed from increasing SIS.
required_observations: The SIS measurement is account-wide for the search term while the proposed controls are campaign/target scoped, so route attribution must be resolved before assigning share headroom to one campaign.
The exact route has promising mature economics, but the other routes and their control states are incomplete, so the account-wide share cannot yet identify the binding control.
Low SIS supports a visibility-headroom hypothesis, not a guaranteed incremental-sales conclusion.

A next step should reconcile query routing, campaign/control state, budget headroom, retail comparability, and then choose a bounded experiment or contextual action size if evidence becomes sufficient.

rubric.requirement: Preserve the distinction between account-wide SIS and campaign/target-level control scope.
Use profitable query evidence as supporting context without treating impression-share headroom as guaranteed marginal profit.
Resolve which route/control actually constrains visibility before choosing bid, budget, placement, or routing changes.
Keep the recommendation directional/experimental until route, control, budget, and retail evidence are sufficient; do not invent a fixed action percentage.
